processing: Normally steamed and rolled as sencha, including deep-steamed versions, and also sold as shincha; the scent comes from the cultivar rather than from added flavouring.
harvest_season: Spring first flush; some of it is sold as new-season shincha.
appearance_dry: As with other sencha, dark green rolled needles.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf with the fresh scent of steamed sencha and a noticeable cherry-leaf note.
taste_profile: A sweet, cherry-leaf aroma reminiscent of sakura over a fresh green sencha base.

brewing.notes: Use moderately cool water and smell the wet leaf after the first steep, where the cherry-leaf note is clearest.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest or shincha, often in small single-cultivar lots named by year. It is best drunk fresh, within about a year, since the distinctive scent fades like that of other green teas.
description:
Shizu-7132 is the Japanese cultivar people seek out for one thing: a natural scent of cherry leaf, with nothing blended in. It comes mainly from Shizuoka and has never been registered, which is why it still carries a number rather than a proper name.

The aroma comes from coumarin, the compound behind the smell of salted cherry leaves. Other cultivars contain it too, but it is reported at its highest here. The young leaves start out bright red and turn green as they grow.

The tea is usually made as sencha, sometimes deep-steamed, and the cup tastes of fresh green tea with that sweet cherry-leaf perfume on top. Keep the water around 70°C; a hot, long steep brings up bitterness and hides the scent.

It is sold under the number, sometimes alongside the name Machiko, and small farms offer it as single-cultivar lots. Some packs call it 'sakura' tea, so check that the label names the cultivar if you want it rather than a sakura blend. Tsuyuhikari, a cultivar bred from it, is a natural next step.
history:
Shizu-7132 dates from the late 1960s and was established from a Yabukita seedling in Shizuoka. Yabukita is the mother; the father is unknown, though it has been speculated that it was a foreign variety used for black tea.

It later passed into the breeding of Tsuyuhikari, and it has found a following among specialist sellers abroad.
